text:
**It’s reasonable to raise the all-male panel as a concern, but it isn’t, by itself, proof that the decision was discriminatory.** It may raise questions about how the municipality ensures fair recruitment; whether it breached any rule depends on your jurisdiction and its hiring policies.

Your qualifications and progress through the interviews give you good reason to seek a substantive explanation. But the announcement is too brief to establish that the successful candidate was less qualified overall. Leadership, management and public-consultation experience may have carried considerable weight. Equally, if a master’s degree or professional licence was an **essential requirement** that he did not meet, that would warrant closer scrutiny.

I would focus on the process rather than the panel’s gender alone:

- **Follow up in writing now**, referring to your earlier request and asking when you can expect a response.
- Ask for the selection criteria, their weightings, and feedback on how your application and interviews were assessed. Ask what recruitment and panel-composition policies applied.
- Keep the advert, job description, correspondence, announcement and your interview notes—particularly any comments about gender, age or family responsibilities.

You could write:

> I’m following up on my request of [date] for written feedback on the appointment. Please explain how my qualifications and interview performance were assessed against the selection criteria, including any essential professional requirements. I would also appreciate confirmation of the policies governing panel composition and how fairness and consistency were ensured.

Two weeks without a reply merits a reminder, but doesn’t itself indicate discrimination. If you’re considering a formal challenge, **check local complaint deadlines promptly**; waiting for feedback may not pause them.

What country or state/province is the municipality in? That will determine whether panel-balance rules, rights to reasons or specific complaint routes apply.
